title: Autonomy, Authority and Anarchy: Creating a Better School Culture 23, 2025
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer uses a composite case study -- 'Schoolington Academy,' where leaders describe a strict Teaching and Learning policy on Cold Call and mini-whiteboards that turns out to be followed in only a minority of the 20 lessons he observes -- to argue that what looks like teacher 'autonomy' in many schools is actually anarchy: a gap between de jure policy and de facto practice with no organising principle at all. Drawing on the etymology of autonomy (self-law, from Greek autos and nomos) versus anarchy (without a ruler), Boxer distinguishes genuine autonomy -- decisions grounded in a teacher's own considered values -- from mere inconsistency produced by weak systems and cultural drift. He contrasts Schoolington with a second fictional school, The Critical Thinking School Academy, which has fully and deliberately embraced teacher autonomy; Boxer argues that even this coherent, values-driven autonomy fails at scale because students who see ten-plus teachers a week cannot cope with radically inconsistent approaches, however well-intentioned each individual teacher's reasoning. His proposed solution is framing school-wide directives as 'prerequisites' rather than 'non-negotiables' -- heteronomous rules that are explicitly grounded in shared values -- combined with departmental-level autonomy, where subject teams collectively decide how to meet a shared prerequisite in ways that respect disciplinary differences.
points: Boxer's central diagnostic tool is the de jure/de facto distinction: many schools have policies (de jure) that bear little resemblance to classroom reality (de facto), and this gap -- not any deliberate teacher choice -- is what he calls anarchy, not autonomy.

He argues true autonomy is defined by self-law grounded in values (moral-philosophy sense), and that Schoolington Academy's inconsistency reflects 'cultural inertia and organisational ineffectiveness' rather than teachers making deliberate value-based choices.

Even fully coherent, values-driven teacher autonomy (The Critical Thinking School Academy) fails at scale, Boxer argues, because a student facing ten-plus teachers a week cannot cope with radically different approaches, however well each is individually justified.

His proposed fix -- 'prerequisites' rather than 'non-negotiables,' plus departmental (not just individual) autonomy -- aims to preserve the motivational benefits of autonomy while still guaranteeing baseline consistency for students.

Boxer explicitly credits a named practitioner (Thanos Gidaropoulos) for the departmental-autonomy framing, grounding the theoretical argument in a specific real-world collaboration rather than presenting it as purely his own invention.
quotes: In three lessons we saw mini-whiteboards, and in the remainder they were not in use when they could have been. In every lesson, we saw students calling out answers and teachers relying on students with their hands up.
This radical disjunct between “what we say” and “what we do” acts as an insurmountable barrier to building a high performing and professional school culture.
The etymology of anarchy is an, meaning “without”, and arkhos, meaning “ruler.” It describes a situation in which nobody is in charge or ruling over anyone else.

The anarchy in Schoolington Academy isn’t deliberate or the result of defiance, nor does it necessarily result in a chaotic or unsafe environment. Instead, it stems from the gradual decay of weak systems and organisational culture, and results in a pedagogic incoherence.

A radically autonomous system like this doesn't work not only because people will make poor decisions but also because it can't scale. Schools are big organisations with lots of people, and a student who has over ten teachers across 30 lessons a week will struggle with this level of inconsistency.

Autonomy might be desirable, but its not an end in and of itself. Autonomy’s ultimate purpose is better outcomes for students, and in failing to achieve these outcomes The Critical Thinking School Academy does not help us in our quest for a better school culture.
